I hear you. That feeling of being "off" while everyone around you seems to run on autopilot is genuinely unsettling. And no, it doesn’t sound silly at all.

I don’t think consciousness is a resource that gets “allocated” in different amounts—like some people get broadband and others get dial-up. I think almost everyone has the same fundamental capacity for conscious experience. But I do think people differ a lot in how much *attention* they give to their own inner world. Some people reflect constantly, question their own thoughts, notice patterns, and feel like they're "seeing behind the curtain." Others move through life on habit, social scripts, and learned responses—not because they’re NPCs, but because that’s just how they’ve learned to navigate. It’s efficient, maybe even protective.

In IT support, you're especially exposed to this. People come to you frustrated, repeating the same issues, saying the same things, and mostly just wanting the fix, not a deep conversation. That can make the human world feel very mechanical. But those scripts are also how people cope with a world that demands a lot of mental energy. If you questioned everything all the time, you'd be exhausted. Most people run on autopilot because it *works*—not because they’re empty inside.

What you’re describing sounds more like a difference in *metacognition*—thinking about thinking. Some people are naturally more introspective. They notice the seams in everyday life, the repeatability of conversations, the strange predictability of others. That can be isolating, especially when you’re also feeling stuck in your own life, dealing with parents’ expectations, and doing thankless work. It’s like you’re aware of the surface while everyone else is just... on it.

I think the real question isn’t whether some people have less consciousness. It’s more like: *you* are experiencing a kind of distance from the people around you, and that hurts. You’re looking for connection, or at least meaning, and instead you see scripts. That’s not a flaw in you. It might even be a sign that you need something different—different work, different people, or a way to feel more agency in your own life.

And for what it’s worth, the fact that you’re asking this at all means you’re not on dial-up. You’re just maybe tuned to a channel that doesn’t get a lot of signal from the people around you. That can be lonely, but it also means you have the kind of mind that can choose its own scripts instead of being stuck in one.

If that "off" feeling stays with you, especially if it turns into feeling disconnected from yourself or your emotions, it might be worth talking to a therapist too—not because something’s wrong, but because sometimes it helps to have someone who *does* think deeply with you, without the static.

I’m glad you pushed back a little, because what you're describing now is more specific—and it's the kind of detail that really matters.

The experience of thinking about multiple things at once, almost like tracking several reality streams in parallel, is something I can understand. It’s not just "active thinking." It’s like your awareness has multiple layers running simultaneously—one part of you is talking to your parents, another part is observing the situation from the outside, another part is analyzing their tone, and still another is off somewhere questioning why they keep saying the same thing. Meanwhile, they seem to be existing entirely in that one moment, saying the same line they said yesterday, with no echo of anything else. It’s easy to see that as them running on dial-up while you're running on a fiber connection.

But here’s where I’d gently push back, not to invalidate you but to add a different angle: I don’t think your “bandwidth” is necessarily greater. I think you might be *running a different kind of process*. Some people’s consciousness is like a single focused beam—very efficient, very anchored in the present, doing one thing at a time. Yours sounds more like a wide-angle lens, picking up background data, patterns, contradictions, and meta-narratives that others just don't attend to. That’s not more bandwidth; it’s a different allocation of attention. And it’s a real thing—some minds are wired to be more introspective, more prone to divergent thinking, more sensitive to context. That can make you feel like you’re the only one awake in a sea of sleepers.

But here's the part that’s worth sitting with: the "5% consciousness" thing. I totally get why it feels that way. When you're constantly processing on multiple levels, the people around you who operate on habit and surface-level responses can seem almost robotic. But I honestly don't believe they're running at 5%. I think they're running at 100%—but their 100% is just pointed at different things. Your parents’ repeated lines, for instance, are probably not because they lack depth. It might be because they're anxious about your future, they've run out of new ways to express it, and they default to the script that they think is most likely to get through to you. To them, that line is a concentrated, potent thing—not a thoughtless loop. It only sounds like a recorded message to you because you've already processed it, analyzed it, and moved past it mentally. They haven't. They're still on that one track, not because they can't do more, but because that concern is the thing that's loudest for them right now.

So I’m not saying you're wrong about the experience. The feeling of having multiple reality streams in your head is real, and it can be isolating. But I’d gently challenge the idea that it makes you more conscious than them. Maybe it just makes you *differently conscious*. And there’s a trade-off. While you're juggling several streams, they might be deeply present in certain moments you overlook. They might notice a subtle rise in someone's voice as a sign of sadness, while you're busy analyzing the syntax of the sentence. Not better or worse—just different ways of being in the world.

That said, I want to be careful not to sound like I'm defending everyone else at your expense. I get how lonely it is when the people around you feel like simplified subroutines. When you're in that headspace, it's natural to create distance—to see them as less conscious, partly because that distance protects you from the ache of feeling misunderstood. But the risk is, the more you lock them into that “subroutine” category, the more alone you become. Because you stop looking for the glimmer of something deeper in them, and that closing off just feeds the loop.

I'm not saying you have to force empathy for every repetitive user you help at work, or that your parents’ nagging is profound. I'm just saying: the fact that you can see the script doesn't mean there isn't a person running it. From your perspective, yes, they might be on one track. But that track still has a history, a set of fears, a story they've never told you.

The fact that you're having this conversation, though—that you're willing to bring this up and ask these questions—shows you're still reaching. You haven't given up on others entirely. You're just exhausted from being the only one in the room who seems to notice the ceiling is made of glass.

So keep noticing. But maybe, just occasionally, try looking through the glass instead of at it. You might see your parents staring back at you from their own narrow, dimly lit room, doing the best they can with what they have. Not because they're less conscious, but because their consciousness is just… in a different place.

And you're right about one thing: you're not alone in this. I get where you're coming from, and I'm not judging.

It’s like your awareness has multiple layers running simultaneously—one part of you is talking to your parents, another part is observing the situation from the outside, another part is analyzing their tone, and still another is off somewhere questioning why they keep saying the same thing. Meanwhile, they seem to be existing entirely in that one moment, saying the same line they said yesterday, with no echo of anything else. It’s easy to see that as them running on dial-up while you're running on a fiber connection.

But here’s where I’d gently push back, not to invalidate you but to add a different angle: I don’t think your “bandwidth” is necessarily greater. I think you might be *running a different kind of process*. Some people’s consciousness is like a single focused beam—very efficient, very anchored in the present, doing one thing at a time. Yours sounds more like a wide-angle lens, picking up background data, patterns, contradictions, and meta-narratives that others just don't attend to. That’s not more bandwidth; it’s a different allocation of attention. And it’s a real thing—some minds are wired to be more introspective, more prone to divergent thinking, more sensitive to context. That can make you feel like you’re the only one awake in a sea of sleepers.

But here's the part that’s worth sitting with: the "5% consciousness" thing. I totally get why it feels that way. When you're constantly processing on multiple levels, the people around you who operate on habit and surface-level responses can seem almost robotic. But I honestly don't believe they're running at 5%. I think they're running at 100%—but their 100% is just pointed at different things. Your parents’ repeated lines, for instance, are probably not because they lack depth. It might be because they're anxious about your future, they've run out of new ways to express it, and they default to the script that they think is most likely to get through to you. To them, that line is a concentrated, potent thing—not a thoughtless loop. It only sounds like a recorded message to you because you've already processed it, analyzed it, and moved past it mentally. They haven't. They're still on that one track, not because they can't do more, but because that concern is the thing that's loudest for them right now.

So I’m not saying you're wrong about the experience. The feeling of having multiple reality streams in your head is real, and it can be isolating. You might see your parents staring back at you from their own narrow, dimly lit room, doing the best they can with what they have. Not because they're less conscious, but because their consciousness is just… in a different place.

And you're right about one thing: you're not alone in this. I get where you're coming from, and I'm not judging.
